metadata.description: A working prototype and build-vs-buy assessment of the three Power Apps workloads.

home.title: Internal Tool Platform Assessment
home.intro: This assessment pairs a working prototype of the three Power Apps workloads with an evaluation of what replacing the platform would take, and concludes with a recommendation.
home.tryIt: To compare role behavior, switch between Viewer, Approver, and Admin in the top-right.
home.assessmentIntro: The analysis behind the recommendation, in three parts: research, evaluation, and recommendation.
home.prototypeNote: Prototype note: data is stored in memory and reseeds on restart; this scope decision is discussed in the evaluation.
home.researchDescription: What Power Apps provides, and which capabilities the three apps rely on.
home.evaluationDescription: What the prototype replicated, what it didn't, and what closing the gap would cost.
home.recommendationDescription: The build-vs-buy recommendation and the reasoning behind it.

sso.name: Real SSO
sso.takes: Managed provider (Auth0, Clerk, WorkOS). Days to integrate, permanent dependency.

database.name: Persistent database
database.takes: Postgres plus migrations, backups, retention. Days to set up, ongoing operations.

connectors.name: Connectors
connectors.takes: Hand-built integrations or an integration layer (Composio, Merge, Paragon). The hardest gap: ongoing work either way.

citizen.name: Citizen development
citizen.takes: Every new tool and every change becomes an engineering ticket.

compliance.name: Compliance certification
compliance.takes: Inherited from infrastructure choices; months of audit work if certification is required.

build.title: Build cost
points: Engineering hours first: hardening the prototype into a production system (SSO, database, integrations, testing) is weeks of senior time, not hours.
Building still means buying: workflow engines (Temporal, Inngest), managed auth, and integration layers each have a bill.
Self-hosting the open-source equivalents trades subscriptions for cloud spend. There is no zero-vendor option.

maintenance.title: Maintenance burden
points: Connectors are a product, not a feature; someone must keep every integration working as third-party APIs change.
Self-hosted infrastructure adds patching, upgrades, and on-call.

security.title: Security implications
points: Authentication (SSO, sessions, MFA) and authorization (role models, permission checks on every action) come with the platform today and would become the team's responsibility.
In a regulated fintech, so do audit and compliance obligations.

opportunity.title: Opportunity cost
points: Citizen development disappears: operations and compliance stop building their own apps and file tickets instead.

Demand forecast decides the scale: at three to ten CRUD apps the current team absorbs it; beyond that, one to three dedicated engineers at $200K+ exceed the license cost before opportunity cost is counted.

capexOpex.title: Capex vs. Opex
capexOpex.intro: The same dimensions, split into one-time and recurring cost.

build.capex: Initial build: weeks of senior engineering to harden the prototype
build.opex: Tool subscriptions or cloud spend for self-hosted equivalents

security.opex: Access reviews, dependency patching, audit and compliance work

opportunity.capex: Features not shipped during the initial build
opportunity.opex: Every tool change as an engineering ticket; 1 to 3 dedicated engineers ($200K+ each) if demand grows

capexOpex.buyProfile: Buying inverts the profile: near-zero capex and a single opex line.
capexOpex.buyOpex: Platform license; the vendor carries maintenance and security

evaluationPage.title: Evaluation
evaluationPage.lead: The prototype was built in roughly two hours with Devin. The goal was to replicate the capability core the three apps use on the platform, not a production system.

researchPage.title: Research
researchPage.lead: What Microsoft Power Apps does, which capabilities the three apps use, and where the platform's value lies.

canvas.name: Canvas apps
canvas.provides: Drag-and-drop UI builder with Excel-like formulas (Power Fx).

modelDriven.name: Model-driven apps
modelDriven.provides: UI generated from the data model: define tables and rules, get grids, forms, and dashboards. The mode used for CRUD internal tools.

dataverse.name: Microsoft Dataverse
dataverse.provides: Managed data platform: relational tables, column-level security, validation, change auditing.

connectors.name: Connectors
connectors.provides: 1,000+ prebuilt integrations; custom connectors for internal APIs.

ai.name: AI / Copilot
ai.provides: Natural-language app generation, AI Builder models.

capabilities.title: The capabilities the three apps use

grids.name: Data grids
grids.detail: Sortable, filterable views over KYC cases, refunds, flags.

forms.name: Validated forms
forms.detail: Required fields, typed inputs, business rules.

rbac.name: RBAC
rbac.detail: Analysts review, compliance leads approve, engineering toggles flags. Required in a regulated fintech.

audit.name: Audit trail
audit.detail: Every change logged with old and new values. Required for KYC and refunds.

approvals.name: Approvals
approvals.detail: Pending / approved / rejected state machines with notifications.

connectors.name: Connectors
connectors.detail: Integrations (identity providers, payment processors) the team does not maintain.

managed.name: Managed platform
managed.detail: SSO, hosting, patching, backups are the vendor's problem.

capabilities.note: Same pattern in all three apps: table, form, role-gated action, audit log. Offline mobile, AI Builder, and the rest of the platform go unused.

value.title: Where the value lies
value.intro: The value is the bundle, not any single feature.

speed.name: Speed
speed.detail: A working CRUD app in hours or days, without engineers.

citizen.name: Citizen development
citizen.detail: Operations and compliance build their own apps.

governance.name: Governance
governance.detail: SSO, RBAC, auditing, SOC 2 / ISO 27001 inherited from Microsoft.

integrations.name: Maintained integrations
integrations.detail: Connectors are configuration, not code to own.

licensing.name: Licensing
licensing.detail: ~$20/user/month list, but premium connectors, Dataverse capacity, and per-app stacking make real costs hard to predict.

delegation.name: Delegation limits
delegation.detail: Non-delegable queries run client-side on 500 to 2,000 rows and return wrong results at scale.

lockin.name: Lock-in
lockin.detail: Apps, Power Fx, and Dataverse data are not portable.

caution.title: Caution: price may not reflect usage
caution.body: Platform spend often reflects contract structure, not usage. At list price, 60 users cost roughly $14.4K/year, far below the reported $250K. Start with a license audit. Compare building against the renegotiated price or a cheaper competitor, not the current contract.

recommendationPage.title: Recommendation
recommendationPage.bluf: Renegotiate or replace the contract first. Build only if that fails, or when demand for internal tools outgrows three apps.

situation.title: Situation
situation.body: The engineering team pays $250K/year for a platform running three CRUD apps. At list price, 60 users cost roughly $14.4K/year. The prototype proves the capability core is replicable in hours. The real cost of building is ownership: SSO, database, connector upkeep, compliance, and the loss of citizen development.

renegotiate.name: Renegotiate the contract
renegotiate.cost: List price is ~$14.4K; even 3x that is far below today

vendor.name: Move to a cheaper vendor (Retool, Appsmith, Budibase)
vendor.effort: Weeks of migration for three small apps

build.name: Build in-house
build.cost: Tool subscriptions now; $200K+ per dedicated engineer if demand grows
build.effort: Weeks of hardening, then permanent upkeep
build.risk: Security and compliance become the team's problem

commodity.name: Commodity test
commodity.detail: Internal CRUD tools do not differentiate the business. Commodity capability defaults to buy.

tco.name: Honest TCO
tco.detail: Build estimates for internal tooling overrun 2.5 to 3x. Compare three-year build cost against the corrected license price, not the current contract. Build only wins against the inflated number.

hybrid.name: There is no pure build
hybrid.detail: Auth, database, and integration layers would still be bought. The real choice is which vendor set to own.

citizen.name: Citizen development is lost
citizen.detail: Today operations and compliance ship their own changes; in-house, every change is an engineering ticket.

devin.name: Where Devin fits
devin.detail: The prototype took two hours, and the follow-on work is the same shape of well-scoped task. Building gets cheaper, but the ownership costs remain.

triggers.title: What would change the call
triggers.intro: The recommendation flips toward build if any of these hold.

audit.name: The audit fails
audit.detail: Spend cannot be brought near list price.

demand.name: Demand grows
demand.detail: A roadmap of ten or more internal tools makes dedicated ownership worth it.

customization.name: Customization becomes a constraint
customization.detail: Delegation limits or UX ceilings block the workflows.

compliance.name: Compliance requires data control
compliance.detail: The vendor cannot provide the required data control.

audit.name: License and usage audit
audit.detail: One week, finance plus one engineer.

quotes.name: Competitor quotes
quotes.detail: Quotes from two competitor platforms, same week.

checkpoint.name: Decision checkpoint
checkpoint.detail: Renegotiated total under roughly $50K/year means buy, and the question closes for a year.

pilot.name: Four-week build pilot with Devin
pilot.detail: Production-harden the KYC app end to end, including SSO and persistence, and re-measure the cost line before committing to the other two.

architecturePage.title: Architecture Overview
architecturePage.lead: How the prototype is built and why: the shape of the system, the key decisions and their tradeoffs, and what the architecture deliberately does not claim.

shape.title: Shape of the System
shape.body: A single Next.js 15 (App Router) application containing the three internal apps, a cross-app audit log, and the written assessment. One repo, one deploy target (Vercel, plus a Docker image for local runs), zero external services. That was deliberate: the exercise is a ~2-hour prototype whose job is to demonstrate the Power Apps capability core, so every piece of infrastructure that did not serve that demonstration was cut.
shape.storeLine: In-memory store (module-level singleton, seeded on boot)

store.name: In-memory store instead of a database
store.detail: A seeded, module-level singleton holds all data; every mutation goes through it and appends an audit entry with before/after values. Cost: data resets on cold starts. Benefit: the whole data layer took minutes, and the workflows, validation, and audit semantics are fully real. Swapping in Postgres later changes one module, not the apps. This is the single most important scope cut, disclosed on the home page and in the evaluation.

auth.name: Mock identity, real authorization
auth.detail: A demo-role cookie plus a role switcher stands in for SSO; building real auth in two hours would have consumed the budget while proving little. But authorization is enforced server-side in every API route, not just hidden in the UI: switching roles genuinely changes what the API permits. Identity is fake, access control is not.

ux.name: Deliberately mirroring Power Apps UX
ux.detail: The shell (top app bar, sitemap sidebar, command bars, view selectors, full-page records) copies model-driven Power Apps on purpose, based on a discovery pass over Microsoft's documentation. A fair build-vs-buy comparison requires the prototype to resemble what the team already runs; a prettier but alien UI would bias it.

docs.name: Assessment lives in the app
docs.detail: Research, evaluation, recommendation, and this overview ship with the artifact they analyze, rendered as designed pages from per-locale message catalogs, with the source documents kept in the repo.

boring.name: Everything else is boring on purpose
boring.detail: TypeScript throughout, shadcn/ui on semantic design tokens (one palette change point, dark mode nearly free), next-intl with per-locale catalogs and doc translations, Intl.* for dates and currency. These choices maximized what two hours could produce and left obvious seams (store, auth) where production concerns would slot in.

limits.title: What This Architecture Does Not Claim
limits.body: No persistence, no real identity provider, no connectors to external systems, no delegated admin or environment management. Those are exactly the Power Apps capabilities whose replacement cost the evaluation prices out; the prototype's job was to make that gap concrete, not to close it.
